1:
The chapter stands where it does on purpose, and Ellicott says why: the Day of Atonement had just purged the community and presented them a holy nation, so it is followed by regulations for every-day life whose observance keeps up the holiness that day secured. Keil heads the next four chapters with the sentence that Israel is not to walk in the way of the heathen but in the ordinances of Jehovah, and treats this one as holiness of food, tying what a man eats to his calling as one of a holy nation. Ellicott then makes an observation nobody else makes, and it turns on a phrase easily read past. The words unto all the children of Israel appear here for the first time; he sets out the seven earlier patterns of divine communication and shows that here alone the high priest and the priesthood are put on a level with the ordinary Israelite as far as this regulation goes. He notes the phrase recurs only twice more, and that the added formula about what the Lord commanded marks the weight of what follows.

What the law forbids divides them: how wide does the word killeth reach? Ellicott holds it covers the three sacrificial quadrupeds when meant for private use, arguing from the vocabulary, since the text says killeth and not sacrificeth, and from comparing these verses with the eighth and ninth. Wesley takes the opposite line, that it is not for common use at all, since such beasts might be killed by anyone anywhere, but for sacrifice only. Henry reports the widest reading, that in the wilderness the people might not kill so much as a lamb for their own table except at the door, a view he says a learned man of his day maintained, holding the rule was altered on entering Canaan. Clarke reaches the same alteration from the practical side: while encamped the thing was easy to enforce, but once settled in the land the distance made it impossible, and they were permitted to pour the blood out at their own dwellings and cover it. On the penalty they agree and are severe. Keil says the slaughtering was reckoned as blood-guiltiness and punished with extermination; Ellicott, that the man is treated as wantonly shedding blood; Wesley, that he is punished as a murderer, because the blood, though not a man's, was sacred and appropriated to God. Clarke sharpens it: that blood, properly employed, might have atoned for the life of a man.

The reason given at the seventh verse takes them all into Egypt. Ellicott glosses the word rendered devils as hairy or shaggy goats, and so goat-shaped deities, tracing the cult to the temple at Thmuis where the goat-image was worshipped; from that stock he derives Pan and Silenus, the satyrs and fauns, and then the horned and cloven-footed devil of medieval Christianity, adding that the terror of that apparition has left us the word panic. Clarke follows the same road with his own authorities: the word means the hairy ones, Pan was figured with the hindquarters and horns and ears of a goat, and Herodotus reports all goats worshipped in Egypt, the he-goat particularly. Henry takes the goat shape as the form in which the evil spirits appeared to invite the sacrifices, and says the devil has coveted divine honours ever since he revolted, having had the impudence to ask them of our Saviour himself. On the whoredom, Clarke insists the word is not merely figurative here, since public prostitution formed a real part of such worship; Henry keeps it figurative, a breach of covenant as adultery breaks a marriage. Gill doubts Israel would descend so far and takes devils for idols in general, though he reports the Zemes that Columbus found in Hispaniola. Keil ends where the text does, with sacrifice confined to one door.
10:
The prohibition is old by the time it reaches this verse. Ellicott observes it has been laid down twice already, both times tied to the prohibition of fat, and is enacted separately here because of its importance; the later rabbinic canons, he adds, exempted the blood of clean fishes, locusts and the permitted creeping things. Henry marks the sheer repetition: a great stress is laid upon it, as a law with more in it than one would think at first view. On the penalty they are agreed and unusually grave. Ellicott glosses the setting of the face as making a man feel the divine anger, showing from other passages that the word carries anger visible in the countenance. Calvin presses what is peculiar in the threat, that God does not merely prescribe to the judges but reserves the office of punishment to himself, so the offender is not safe though he escape the bench. Wesley gives the practical ground: such a thing would likely be done in private, where no magistrate could reach it. Henry's summary is the one Wesley then repeats almost word for word, that the man against whom God sets his face is undone, for ever undone, since no creature can confront his Creator.

The eleventh verse gives the reason, and Ellicott begins by correcting the rendering. The word translated life occurs twice more in the same verse and is both times given as soul; either will do, but one must be used throughout, the older version having needlessly increased the difficulty by varying it. What is asserted is that the blood is the principle of vitality and constitutes the soul of animal life, so that blood and life stand interchangeably in Scripture. Clarke turns this into a scientific claim, observing that the sentence stood here for thirty-six centuries before any philosopher attended to it, and that a celebrated anatomist of his own day revived the Mosaic notion of the vitality of the blood and established it by experiment: that blood unites living parts, that it becomes vascular, that drawn in extreme cold it raises the thermometer as high as blood drawn in heat, and that severing the nerve to a limb only paralyses it while severing the artery kills it. Gill reaches for the same authority independently, calling the blood the first that lives and the last that dies. Henry keeps the point sacrificial rather than medical: the sinner deserved to die, therefore the sacrifice must die, and the blood on the altar signified the life given to God instead of the sinner's.

Two questions follow. The first is who the strangers are. Calvin will not take them for every visitor on business, but for those who had devoted themselves to the worship of God, many foreigners having abandoned their superstitions and been circumcised; he notes that heathen sojourners were not under the prohibition at all, being allowed to buy even flesh torn by beasts. Ellicott gives a different reason: they had submitted to the law of the land, and their eating blood would lessen the horror with which the Jews regarded it. The second question is whether the law still binds, and here they part. Henry says the reason given in the text is now superseded, which shows the law was ceremonial and is no longer in force, the blood of Christ alone now making atonement. Calvin accounts for the apostolic decree differently: because the patriarchs had abstained before the Law was given, the Apostles did not dare permit blood at once when they abrogated the ceremonial law, lest so new a liberty cause scandal. Ellicott simply records the enforcement in Acts. Wesley gives the double reason: to eat it was to eat up the ransom of their own lives, and it was irreverence toward the blood of Christ which it represented. Gill adds only that the rule held for great and small alike.
13:
The law now widens, and Ellicott marks the step: up to this point it has dealt with sacrificial animals and with the quadrupeds a man kills at home, and here it is extended to every other creature that is wild but legally clean and used for food. He explains why hunters in particular needed the rule. Hunting was an amusement among other ancient nations but a necessity with the Hebrews, resorted to for destroying dangerous beasts and more especially for procuring food, by pitfalls and snares as well as weapons; and a man who has wounded his game, or must kill it on the spot to carry it home, is exactly the man likely to grow careless about the blood. He gives the practice the law was aimed against, that the Zabians on slaying a beast put its blood into a vessel or a hole dug in the ground and sat round it to feast, and he points to the hungry army in the book of Samuel that flew upon the spoil and ate the flesh with the blood. Gill notes only that the double address, to Israelites and to the strangers among them, is the form used throughout to fix whom the law binds.

The fourteenth verse states the ground again, and Keil renders it so that the clause actually reasons: the case with the soul of all flesh is that its blood makes out its soul. On that footing he draws the practical rule, that even in animals never fit for the altar the blood was to be let run upon the ground and then covered with earth, or, as he puts it, buried. Ellicott would keep soul rather than life throughout, and offers a second possible rendering, that the life of all flesh consists in its blood during its life, but only while the blood still holds it, since once dried or coagulated the life has passed out. Clarke, having granted the moral reason, adds four of his own from natural philosophy: that blood is highly alkalescent and in hot climates putrefies quickly; that it is gross and hard nutriment, so indigestible that the blood of bulls was used by the ancients as a poison; that where it was eaten in quantity scurvy was commoner; and that the nations which lived most upon it proved the fiercest, the Scythians and Tartars and Scandinavians among them, some of whom drank the blood of their enemies out of their skulls.

The last two verses follow from the same principle: a beast that died of itself or was torn keeps much of its blood in it, and is therefore forbidden, such carcases being thrown to the dogs. He notes that the later canon extended the ban to whatever died naturally, by accident, by strangling or by a wild beast, which explains the apostolic decree about things strangled; Clarke reaches the same conclusion by the same road, that the blood was coagulated in the veins. Gill measures the offence exactly, that a man broke the law by eating so much as an olive's bulk, and reports that Grotius traced the Pythagorean rule against animals that died of themselves to this very statute. On who is bound, Ellicott and Wesley agree that the proselyte is included while the mere stranger outside the community was left free to eat such things. On the penalty they differ. Wesley takes the eating to be through ignorance, since a wilful act was punished more severely, and reads the bearing of iniquity as requiring a sacrifice; Gill, following Jarchi, assigns cutting off for the unwashed body and a beating for the unwashed clothes; Ellicott distinguishes rather by the offence, excision for entering the sanctuary defiled and stripes for eating of the holy meal. Clarke closes the chapter with a plain remark, that there is as little propriety in eating blood as there is necessity for it.
